lead: An optical receiver turns a weak, noisy train of light pulses back into clean bits. In every bit period it must decide whether the light was on or off, and it must do so at a stated error rate with as little power as possible. The chain is always the same: photodiode, low-noise preamplifier, main amplifier and equaliser, low-pass filter, and a decision circuit clocked by a recovered timing signal. Its key specification is the sensitivity, the weakest average power that still meets the target bit error rate; every link power budget starts from this number.
prereq: You need the noise formulas of Photodetector noise; the Q factor used here is explained in Bit error rate and receiver performance.

sections.h3: The chain from photon to bit

blocks.text: A receiver does four jobs in order: convert light to current, amplify that current while adding as little noise as possible, shape the pulses so that each bit stays in its own time slot, and decide one or zero near the centre of each slot.

items: Photodiode (PIN or APD): delivers a current I = RP, where R is the responsivity in A/W and P the received optical power in W.
Preamplifier (front end): a low-noise stage that turns the current into a voltage. Its noise usually sets the noise of the whole receiver.
Main amplifier and equaliser: raises the signal to a level the decision circuit can use, and corrects pulse spreading from the fiber and the front end.

Low-pass filter: removes noise outside the signal band. For NRZ data at bit rate B<sub>T</sub> its bandwidth is usually about 0.5B<sub>T</sub> to 0.7B<sub>T</sub>; wider passes more noise, narrower smears neighbouring bits together.
Decision circuit: a comparator that samples the filtered signal once per bit, at t = nT with bit period T = 1/B<sub>T</sub> and bit number n, and outputs 1 if the sample is above the threshold.
Clock recovery: extracts a clock at B<sub>T</sub> from the transitions in the data and times the decision circuit. Without it the sampling point drifts.
Automatic gain control (AGC): a loop that holds the output level steady when the received power changes, so the threshold stays in the right place.

blocks.text: AGC matters because a receiver must work over a dynamic range: the ratio of the strongest to the weakest input it accepts. Too strong a signal overloads the amplifiers, the pulses flatten and errors appear even though there is plenty of light.
The preamplifier sets both the bandwidth and the noise. C<sub>T</sub> is the total input capacitance (photodiode plus amplifier).

blocks.text: In a transimpedance amplifier (TIA) the resistor R<sub>f</sub> sits in the feedback path of an inverting amplifier with open-loop gain A. The output voltage is V = −IR<sub>f</sub>, so the transimpedance is R<sub>f</sub> ohms. Feedback makes the input look like a small resistance R<sub>f</sub>/(A + 1), so the bandwidth is about A times wider than a high-impedance front end with R<sub>L</sub> = R<sub>f</sub>, while the thermal noise is still that of the large R<sub>f</sub>.

blocks.where: B is the closed-loop bandwidth in Hz, A the amplifier's open-loop voltage gain, R<sub>f</sub> the feedback resistance in Ω and C<sub>T</sub> the total input capacitance in F.

blocks.text: Doubling R<sub>f</sub> lowers the noise current by a factor √2 but halves the bandwidth. That trade-off is the design problem of the front end. With R<sub>f</sub> = 10 kΩ, C<sub>T</sub> = 1 pF and A = 20, B ≈ 318 MHz; a high-impedance front end with the same resistor would give only 15.9 MHz.

Sensitivity is the minimum average received optical power needed to reach a stated bit error rate (BER) at a stated bit rate. Without both numbers it means nothing. It is usually quoted in dBm: P(dBm) = 10 log₁₀(P/1 mW), so 1 µW is −30 dBm and 100 nW is −40 dBm.

Take a PIN receiver limited by thermal noise, so that a one and a zero have the same rms noise σ. With on–off keying the zero level is (ideally) zero current. For the target BER the two levels must be Qσ above and below the threshold, so the one level must be I<sub>1</sub> = 2Qσ. The average current is half of that, Qσ, and the average power follows.

blocks.where: P<sub>sens</sub> is the sensitivity as average received power in W; Q is about 6 for BER = 10⁻⁹ and about 7 for 10⁻¹²; σ is the rms noise current in A; R is the responsivity in A/W.

blocks.text: An APD multiplies the signal by M before the preamplifier, while the preamplifier's noise stays the same, but it adds signal-dependent shot noise. For a zero level of zero and thermal noise σ<sub>T</sub>, the sensitivity becomes

F is the excess noise factor at gain M and B the receiver bandwidth. Put M = F = 1 and drop the small shot term to get back Qσ<sub>T</sub>/R. The best M makes this smallest; APD receivers are typically 5 to 10 dB more sensitive than PIN receivers of the same speed.

There is also an absolute floor, the quantum limit. Even an ideal detector with no thermal noise makes an error when a "one" pulse happens to contain no photon. For BER = 10⁻⁹ a one must carry about 20 photons on average, so the average is about 10 photons per bit, whatever the bit rate. At 1.55 µm and 2.5 Gbit/s that is 10 × 1.28 × 10⁻¹⁹ J × 2.5 × 10⁹ s⁻¹ = 3.2 nW (−54.9 dBm). Real receivers sit 20 dB or more above it.

examples.question: A PIN receiver has responsivity R = 0.9 A/W and total input noise current σ = 40 nA rms (about the noise of a 1 kΩ resistor over 100 MHz, as worked out in Photodetector noise). It must reach BER = 10⁻⁹, which needs Q = 6. (a) Find the sensitivity in watts and in dBm, and the one-level current. (b) The fiber and connectors lose 30 dB. What average power must the transmitter launch?
steps: Currents: the average current is RP<sub>sens</sub> = 0.9 × 267 nA = 240 nA = Qσ. The one level is I<sub>1</sub> = 2Qσ = 480 nA, the zero level 0, and the threshold sits at 240 nA, which is 6σ from each level.
Launch power: losses in dB add to the dBm figure, so P<sub>launch</sub> = −35.7 dBm + 30 dB = −5.7 dBm (0.27 mW).
examples.answer: Sensitivity 267 nW, which is −35.7 dBm, with a one level of 480 nA; with 30 dB of loss the transmitter must launch at least −5.7 dBm, before any safety margin.

traps: Quoting a sensitivity without its bit rate and BER. The same receiver is less sensitive at a higher bit rate, because σ grows with √B.
Mixing peak and average power. P<sub>sens</sub> ≈ Qσ/R is the average power; the one level needs twice that.
Losing the dBm reference: 0 dBm is 1 mW, −30 dBm is 1 µW, and every 10 dB is a factor of ten in power.
Writing the transimpedance bandwidth as 1/(2πR<sub>f</sub>C<sub>T</sub>). That is the high-impedance value; feedback makes the TIA about A times wider.
Setting the filter bandwidth equal to the bit rate "to be safe". About 0.5B<sub>T</sub> to 0.7B<sub>T</sub> is enough for NRZ; a wider filter only adds noise.

quiz.q: State the four jobs a receiver performs, in order.
quiz.a: Convert light to current, amplify it with little added noise, shape and filter the pulses, and make a clocked one-or-zero decision in each bit slot.

quiz.q: Why does a high-impedance front end need an equaliser?
quiz.a: Its large load resistor and the input capacitance give a narrow bandwidth, 1/(2πR<sub>L</sub>C<sub>T</sub>), which integrates the pulses. The equaliser boosts the high frequencies to restore the pulse shape; this also limits the dynamic range.

quiz.q: What must a sensitivity specification always state?
quiz.a: The bit rate, the BER, and that the power is the average power; for an APD receiver also the gain or bias used.

quiz.q: A receiver has R = 0.8 A/W, σ = 50 nA rms and needs Q = 6. Find its sensitivity in dBm.
A TIA has R<sub>f</sub> = 10 kΩ, open-loop gain A = 20 and C<sub>T</sub> = 1 pF. Estimate its bandwidth.
In a TIA front end R<sub>f</sub> is doubled. What happens to the noise current and the bandwidth, and when does the change help?
quiz.a: The rms thermal noise current falls by a factor √2, since it goes as √(4k<sub>B</sub>TB/R<sub>f</sub>), and the bandwidth halves, since B ≈ A/(2πR<sub>f</sub>C<sub>T</sub>). It helps only if the halved bandwidth is still about 0.5B<sub>T</sub> to 0.7B<sub>T</sub> or more; otherwise neighbouring bits smear together and the eye closes.

quiz.q: Why does a receiver fail when the input power is too high?
quiz.a: The amplifiers overload and clip, so the pulses flatten and their shape and threshold no longer match. This sets the top of the dynamic range.

quiz.q: How many watts is 0 dBm, and how many is −30 dBm?
quiz.a: 0 dBm = 1 mW = 10⁻³ W; −30 dBm = 1 µW = 10⁻⁶ W.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern receivers put the photodiode, TIA and limiting amplifier in one package, and CMOS and SiGe front ends are routine at 10 Gbit/s and above. Coherent receivers move equalisation and clock recovery into digital signal processing. Burst-mode receivers in passive optical networks must settle their threshold within a few bits of each new packet. Search next for "transimpedance amplifier design", "burst-mode receiver" and "receiver overload".
